Douglas MacArthur. The commanding general of the American forces in the Pacific during World War II and the military administrator of occupied Japan, shaping the post-war order in East Asia. An officer of towering ambition and supreme confidence, he engineered the spectacular Inchon landing in Korea and left an indelible mark on occupied Japan's democratization. His dismissal by President Truman during the Korean War, stemming from their irreconcilable disagreement over strategy and civilian control of the military, made him one of the most controversial figures in American history, epitomizing the tension between military genius and political authority.

Born in 1880 into a military family, MacArthur graduated first in his West Point class and served in multiple campaigns in Mexico and during World War I before rising to prominence in the nineteen-thirties as a senior commander. During World War II, he commanded American forces in the Pacific, implementing the island-hopping strategy that bypassed heavily fortified Japanese positions and struck at isolated targets instead, bringing the war to Japan's home islands. He directed the Aleutian campaign, the Papua New Guinea campaign, and the liberation of the Philippines, fighting back from near-catastrophic defeats to establish American dominance.

In 1945, he accepted Japan's surrender and served as Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers in occupied Japan until 1951, presiding over Japan's transformation from a militaristic empire to a democratic nation. He oversaw land reform, the dissolution of the zaibatsu—the industrial conglomerates—and the drafting of Japan's Peace Constitution.

His most celebrated tactical moment came in September 1950, when he launched the Inchon landing in the Korean War, an amphibious assault at the Inchon port that caught the Communist forces off-guard and turned the tide of an otherwise stalemate conflict. Yet this triumph led to his downfall. He clashed with President Harry Truman over the conduct of the Korean War, particularly over whether to expand the conflict into China. Truman sacked him in April 1951, a stunning moment of civilian authority overruling a celebrated military commander. After leaving office, MacArthur became a hero to the Republican right, returning to testify before Congress and remaining a fixture of American politics until his death in 1964.
